passage:
Sunday, two weeks after. Nikita still couldn't say the words 'the shop closed' without her throat tightening. When Tanuja asked, she said, 'I was useless. I did everything wrong.' A minute later: 'Actually, the courier rates went up, it's not my fault.' Both felt true and neither helped.
Wednesday. Tanuja came over with a notebook and drew three columns: in my control, luck, change next time. Nikita filled them slowly. In control: she never raised prices, and she stopped posting new plants in the monsoon. Luck: the courier rates, the heavy rain in August. Change: price for delivery, keep a small stock, check the numbers monthly. She crossed out 'useless'. It didn't fit any column.
The next Saturday she showed the page to her old supplier, who nodded at the price column and said, 'Yes. That was it.' Nikita felt oddly lighter.

qa.q: What three columns did Tanuja draw?
qa.a: She drew three columns: in my control, luck, change next time.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel 'oddly lighter' on Saturday?
qa.a: She felt relief because seeing the causes clearly turned the failure into something she understood and could fix.

qa.q: What went well in the way Nikita reviewed the closure?
qa.a: She looked fairly at both her own choices and bad luck, instead of either calling herself useless or blaming only the courier.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the change in Nikita between Sunday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Tanuja may feel glad to see her friend move from swinging between blame and excuses to calm, useful thinking.

grounding: It shows a person, after the first pain eases, sorting what was in her control, what was luck and what to change, turning failure into information.

passage:
Sit down, Eshaan. Your Chinmay Chacha has lost more than one pitch, you know.
When I was twenty-four I failed the state services prelims. I didn't leave my room for three days. Then, for weeks, I swung between two stories. Story one: I'm just not smart enough. Story two: the paper was unfair, the questions changed, bad luck.
My old teacher, Joshi-ma'am, made me write a list. Three questions. What was in my hands? I never did full mock tests with a timer. I read, but I didn't practise. What was luck? Yes, the pattern changed that year. Everyone got the same luck, though. What would I change? Timed tests, every Sunday.
That list was the most useful thing I wrote that whole year, Eshaan. Not because it made me feel better. Because it told me what to do.
So. Your pitch. Get a paper.

qa.q: How many days did Chacha not leave his room after failing the prelims?
qa.a: He didn't leave his room for three days.

qa.q: How did Chacha feel during the weeks he swung between two stories?
qa.a: He felt stuck and discouraged, thinking either he wasn't smart enough or it was all bad luck, and neither story let him move forward.

qa.q: What is Chacha advising Eshaan to do about the lost pitch?
qa.a: He wants Eshaan to write down what was in his hands, what was luck and what to change, so the failure turns into clear next steps.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling as his Chacha tells this story?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel comforted that an elder he respects also failed, and ready to look at the pitch honestly instead of just feeling bad.

grounding: It shows an elder describing an honest review of a failure, separating control, luck and change and avoiding both self-blame and excuses.
